start: Cut `[4, 5, 7, 0, 1, 2]` at any midpoint and at least one side is still in plain sorted order. On a sorted side, its two end values tell you at a glance whether the target could be there; if it cannot, it can only be on the other side.

Binary search with inclusive bounds, keeping a present target inside `[lo, hi]` and testing `nums[mid] == target` first. If `nums[lo] <= nums[mid]` the left side is sorted, so keep it only if `target` falls between `nums[lo]` and `nums[mid]`; otherwise the right side is sorted, so keep it only if `target` falls between `nums[mid]` and `nums[hi]`. Validate first: ints, no repeats, and for two or more values exactly one drop between neighbours, counting the wrap from last to first.

start.text: The shape, with the range tests left to you:
start.code:
def rotated_search(nums, target):
    ...  # ValueError checks, including the drops counted around the circle
    lo, hi = 0, len(nums) - 1
    while lo <= hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if nums[mid] == target:
            return mid
        if nums[lo] <= nums[mid]:  # left side sorted
            ...  # keep the left side only if target is in its range
        else:  # right side sorted
            ...
    return -1

test_contract: `[4, 5, 7, 0, 1, 2]` with target 1 gives 4, `[]` gives -1 and `[1]` with target 1 gives 0. Then `[2, 1, 3]`, `[1, 1]`, `[2, 1, 2]`, `[True]` and `[1, 3, 2, 4]` must each raise `ValueError` for target 1, which a plain search finds in every one of them, so validate the whole list before searching.

`[2, 1, 3]` and `[1, 3, 2, 4]` go down only once between neighbours, yet neither is a rotation, because the last value is bigger than the first. Count drops around the circle, last to first included: a rotation of two or more values has exactly one. `[2, 1, 2]` has exactly one as well, so repeats need their own check, and `[True]` needs `type(x) is int`.
test_every_rotation_against_linear_looku: Every rotation of every increasing tuple of up to 6 values from -3 to 3, `()` and single values included, searched for every target from -4 to 4. The inputs are tuples, and many targets are absent, so every path through your search has to end at `-1` rather than at a wrong index.

Two-element windows are where it usually breaks. When `lo == mid`, the left side is the single value `nums[lo]`, which counts as sorted, so the test is `nums[lo] <= nums[mid]`, not `<`: with `<`, `rotated_search((3, 1), 1)` returns -1.

IndexError: `nums[hi]` with `hi = len(nums)`: this search reads both ends of its window, so its bounds are inclusive, `hi = len(nums) - 1`. Reading `nums[0]` or `nums[-1]` also fails on `[]`: return -1 for the empty list before touching it.
ValueError: `min(nums)` fails on the empty input, and `nums.index(target)` fails whenever the target is absent, which the tests ask about constantly. Handle `[]` first, and search instead of calling `.index`.

If it is your own check firing on valid input: “Every rotation against linear lookup” passes tuples. `isinstance(nums, list)` rejects them, and a list from `sorted()` never equals a tuple, so comparing the two always says unsorted.

stopped: With inclusive bounds, `while lo <= hi`, each move must step past `mid`: `lo = mid + 1` or `hi = mid - 1`. `lo = mid` or `hi = mid` leaves a one- or two-element window where `mid` never changes.

If you find the rotation point first, that search has its own trap: with `while lo < hi`, move `lo = mid + 1` when `nums[mid] > nums[hi]` and `hi = mid` otherwise. `lo = mid` never ends, and `hi = mid - 1` can skip the smallest value.
passing: All passing. Try the README's first follow-up, allowing duplicates: `[1, 0, 1, 1, 1]` and `[1, 1, 1, 0, 1]` show the same values at `lo`, `mid` and `hi`, with the 0 on opposite sides. What can your search safely do when it cannot tell which side is sorted, and what does that cost in the worst case?
